editorial:
Picture yourself stepping into smoky Greenwich Village clubs in the early 1960s, where a quiet kid from Minnesota shows up with a guitar and a voice like gravel and poetry mixed together. You follow his rise from unknown kid to the voice of a generation, meeting legends like Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, and Joan Baez along the way. The movie feels like flipping through an old photo album of American music, full of cigarette smoke, protest signs, and songs that still hit hard today. It is less about big plot twists and more about watching a young artist figure out who he wants to be while everyone around him tries to claim him for their own cause.

The acting is the real star, especially the lead performance that captures that strange, slippery charm without becoming an impression. The music sounds great, the costumes feel lived in, and the pacing keeps you moving even when not much happens on screen. On the downside, if you are not into folk music or slow character studies, some stretches may feel long, and a few side characters get shortchanged. Still, music lovers and biopic fans will eat this up.
endingExplained: In the final scenes, Dylan takes the stage at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival and plugs in an electric guitar, shocking the crowd and angering folk purists like Pete Seeger. Boos rain down, but he keeps playing, refusing to be boxed in by what fans expect. The movie ends with him riding off on his motorcycle, leaving behind the folk world that made him famous. The twist is that the hero does not get a triumphant victory lap; instead, he chooses freedom over approval, proving he was never really one of them.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves music biopics and 1960s culture.
